                                   I. INTRODUCTION

Claimant Amy McDougall (McDougall) seeks to exempt her bank accounts from levy

under California Family Code sections 770, 911(a), 1500, and 1612, on the grounds that

the funds are her separate property and not subject to liability for her spouse’s premarital

debt. The judgment creditor, National Collection Agency, Inc. (National), opposes the

claim, contending that McDougall has not adequately proven the separate nature of the

funds. However, National’s objections are unsupported by admissible evidence and fail as

a matter of law. For the reasons set forth below, the Claim of Exemption should be

granted.:


                                                 -1-
      MEMORANDUM OF POINTS AND AUTHORITIES IN SUPPORT OF CLAIM OF EXEMPTION
  1. McDougall’s earnings are protected under Family Code § 911(a). The bank accounts

    containing her earnings are held solely in her name and contain only her separate property.

 2. The judgment creditor bears the burden of proving commingling, and National has failed to do

    so. Mere references to shared financial decisions do not establish that McDougall’s personal

    bank accounts contain community funds.

 3. The Premarital Agreement is valid and dispositive. The agreement explicitly states that no

    community property shall be created. The Memorandum of Understanding (MOU), signed by

    both parties and their attorneys, is sufficient to support McDougall’s claim. National’s request

    for additional documents is unnecessary and unsupported by law.

For these reasons, McDougall respectfully requests that the Court uphold her Claim of Exemption.

                                      II. LEGAL ARGUMENT
              A. McDougall's Bank Funds Are Exempt under Family Code § 911(a)

California Family Code § 911(a) explicitly protects the earnings of a married person from liability for

his or her spouse’s pre-marriage debts, as long as (1) the earnings are held in a separate account

where the non-earning spouse has no right of withdrawal and (2) the funds remain uncommingled

with community property, except for amounts deemed insignificant.

McDougall meets both conditions. She has testified that the bank accounts in question containing her

earnings are separate, that she maintains exclusive control over them, that Mr. Peinado has no
withdrawal rights, and that no funds have been commingled. National has presented no actual

evidence showing that Peinado has access to or control over these funds. Mere speculation does not

meet the burden of proof required to deny an exemption. Furthermore, a valid prenuptial agreement

defining property rights is dispositive. (Fam.Code, § 1500). The property rights of spouses prescribed

by statute may be altered by a premarital agreement or other marital property agreement. In re

Marriage of Bonds (2000) 24 Cal.4th 1, 13; Leasefirst v. Borrelli (1993) 13 Cal. App.4th Supp. 28.)




                                               -2-
          MEMORANDUM OF POINTS AND AUTHORITIES IN SUPPORT OF CLAIM OF EXEMPTION
                B. National Fails to Prove Commingling of Bank Funds

National's arguments rely on isolated statements made by Peinado in an unrelated case (e.g., we put

an offer on the lot, we are developing property together) and McDougall’s name appearing on utility

bills at Peinado’s residence. These facts do not establish commingling. Joint decision-making in real

estate does not equate to shared finances, and such statements are irrelevant to the specific bank

accounts at issue. National has presented no evidence of actual commingling or a valid transmutation

of McDougall’s separate property. Mere references to spousal cooperation do not alter the legal

character of separate assets. (In re Marriage of Weaver (1990) 224 Cal.App.3d 478, 487.) Similarly,

the payment of household expenses is not conclusive proof of commingling. Under California law,

using separate property to pay for household needs does not convert separate assets into community

property. (Weaver, supra; In re Marriage of Braud (1996) 45 Cal.App.4th 797, 822–823; Leasefirst,

supra, 13 Cal.App.4th Supp. at 30–31.) Furthermore, again, a valid prenuptial agreement defining

property rights is dispositive. (Bonds, supra, 24 Cal.4th at 13; Fam.Code, § 1500.)

       C. The Premarital Agreement Supports McDougall’s Claim of Separate Property

McDougall and Peinado executed a Premarital Agreement in 2007, expressly stating that no

community property would be created during the marriage and each spouse’s earnings and property

would remain separate.

California courts uphold prenuptial agreements under Family Code § 1615 unless a party proves

fraud, coercion, or lack of disclosure. National does not argue that any of these apply. Thus, the

agreement is enforceable under California law and conclusively demonstrates that the accounts in

question are the separate property of McDougall. Leasefirst v. Borrelli (1993) 13 Cal.App.4th Supp.

28 held that a wife's separate property did not become community property, and thus was not subject

to levy for her husband's premarital debt, even though she used her wages to support them both. The

court emphasized that a valid prenuptial agreement transmuted the character of the property:


        Furthermore, the trial court held that the explicitly defined separate property of
        Nancy Borrelli changed to community property and was subject to levy on the
        debt of the spouse. The court came to this conclusion based on the fact that
        Nancy Borrelli utilized her wages to support Fred Borrelli and herself. This
        conclusion is contrary to statutory law. The parties here executed a valid written
        prenuptial agreement transmuting what would be presumed community property
        into separate property. (Leasefirst, supra, at 30-31.)

                                                -3-
        MEMORANDUM OF POINTS AND AUTHORITIES IN SUPPORT OF CLAIM OF EXEMPTION
          D. The Judgment Creditor Has Failed to Rebut the Showing of Exemption

Under Code of Civil Procedure section 703.080, once the claimant makes a prima facie showing that

the funds at issue are exempt, the burden shifts to the judgment creditor to rebut that

showing. To date, the creditor has not submitted any evidence disputing the exempt nature of the

funds.

                                       III. CONCLUSION

National’s arguments rely on speculation and irrelevant assertions rather than admissible evidence.

Under Family Code sections 770, 911(a), and 1612, McDougall has demonstrated that the levied

bank account is her separate property and that her earnings are not subject to liability for Peinado’s

premarital debt.

Pursuant to Code of Civil Procedure section 703.580(b), McDougall has met her burden of proof

and is entitled to an exemption.

Accordingly, she respectfully requests that the Court grant her Claim of Exemption and order the

release of the levy on her separate bank account.
